title: How do biotech hedge funds make money? - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Biotech hedge funds (Baker Brothers, Deerfield, OrbiMed, each >$15B) profit partly because many clinical trial outcomes are predictable from public data (Insilico's inClinico hit 79% on 14 Phase II trials), but public-data edges get competed away. The article argues durable edge also comes from expert-network information extraction, exemplified by the Martoma/SAC bapineuzumab insider trade ($275M), and that subtle leakage persists today.

insights.claim: Hundreds of billions of dollars are managed by biotech-specialist hedge funds and investment firms; the largest, Baker Brothers Advisors, Deerfield Management and OrbiMed, each manage over $15 billion.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Specialist biotech capital is concentrated in a few large players whose flows and 13F positioning can move small/mid-cap biotech names.
insights.quote: The largest are Baker Brothers Advisors, Deerfield Management, and OrbiMed, each managing over $15 billion.
insights.locator: And yet, hundreds of billions of dollars

insights.claim: Baker Brothers' roughly twenty-year holding in Seagen, an early antibody-drug-conjugate company, turned about $2 billion into $10 billion, illustrating that top biotech specialists can see long-horizon platform value that is opaque even to peers.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Long-duration conviction in novel modalities (e.g., ADCs) is a key source of specialist-fund returns; tracking long-held specialist positions can flag future platform winners.
insights.quote: consider Baker Brothers’ twenty-year investment in Seagen, one of the first antibody-drug-conjugate companies, an investment which ended up converting $2 billion into $10 billion
insights.locator: But for the most accurate players

insights.claim: A surprisingly large share of clinical trial results are predictable from public information; some expensive trials are run on approaches that have failed badly before and have little reason to succeed.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Trial-readout binary events are not coin flips; systematic analysis of prior failures and trial design can generate edge in pricing catalyst risk.
insights.quote: a surprisingly large number of clinical trial results are actually decently predictable by anyone willing to simply look

insights.claim: Insilico Medicine's inClinico platform, using simple target-choice features (omics data, biomedical knowledge graph) and trial-design features (enrollment size, blinding, number of endpoints, patient age, location, funder type), predicted Phase II outcomes with 79% accuracy across 14 resolved trials in date-stamped preregistered predictions.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Simple ML on public trial metadata can beat base rates on Phase II readouts, though the 14-trial sample is small; quant-style trial forecasting is a viable public-information edge.
insights.quote: hit 79 percent accuracy across 14 resolved trials
insights.locator: Insilico Medicine has published a paper

insights.claim: Biotech hedge funds historically hired small armies of graduate students to compile trial information as table stakes, a function LLMs may now largely replace; RA Capital runs a dedicated division, TechAtlas, for this effort.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: LLMs commoditize public-data compilation in biotech research, eroding that edge and pushing funds toward proprietary or private information sources.
insights.quote: One of the most famous of the pack – RA Capital – has an entire division called ‘TechAtlas’ dedicated to the effort.
insights.locator: LLMs may have replaced a decent chunk

insights.claim: If trial outcomes can be predicted by training a model or analyst on essentially public information, that edge should be competed away, implying persistent biotech fund profits must come partly from somewhere else, such as private information.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Treat claimed public-data edges in biotech skeptically; durable alpha likely depends on information access, not just analysis.
insights.quote: if it’s as easy as training a model or a human on what is essentially public information, how does anybody make money here?
insights.locator: But then we arrive at the same

themes.theme: Expert networks as an information channel

insights.claim: Biotech investors spend heavily on expert networks, paying $500 to $1,000 or more per hour to speak with clinicians, trial investigators or advisory board members about whether specific clinical trials will succeed.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Expert-network spend is a structural cost and moat of biotech investing; retail and generalist investors face an information disadvantage around trial readouts.
insights.quote: They pay an expert network $500 to $1,000 or more per hour
insights.locator: The biotech investing industry spends enormous sums

insights.claim: Expert-network calls are legal, but analysts can read non-verbal cues such as a clinician's hesitation about an endpoint as tradable signal, creating a gray zone between legitimate insight and material non-public information.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The edge in expert calls is often in subtle signals, not explicit disclosure, which regulators struggle to police.
insights.quote: There is nothing stopping you from taking their moment of hesitation as a sign of something worth trading on.
insights.locator: The stated purpose is to gain

insights.claim: Subtle information extraction from scientists persists after the Martoma case: consultations are now more often recorded and experts are warier, but unrecorded private conversations between finance and science friends continue, making the game hard for outsiders to enter.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Assume informed specialist flow ahead of biotech readouts; unusual pre-catalyst positioning by specialist funds may carry signal.
insights.quote: the thing that led to the Martoma prosecution never stopped in any meaningful sense
insights.locator: Now, an interesting question to ask

insights.claim: SEC enforcement functions as a deterrent mainly at the explicit end of insider-information sharing, not against subtle information leakage.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk is concentrated in blatant cases; subtle informational advantages in biotech remain largely unpoliced.
insights.quote: the SEC is not magic, but it has ruined enough lives to function as a deterrent at the explicit end of the spectrum
insights.locator: Now, an interesting question to ask

insights.claim: SAC Capital PM Mathew Martoma, via Gerson Lehrman Group, held dozens of paid consultations over two years with Dr Sidney Gilman, chair of the safety monitoring committee for Alzheimer's drug bapineuzumab; SAC built a ~$700 million long in the two sponsors, then liquidated and went short after Gilman leaked failure in July 2008, netting $275 million in profits and avoided losses.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The largest insider trade in US history ran through a routine expert-network channel, showing where biotech information leakage risk concentrates.
insights.quote: SAC had netted $275 million in combined profits and losses avoided
insights.locator: The main character is Mathew Martoma

insights.claim: Martoma was convicted of securities fraud in 2014; SAC Capital paid $1.8 billion in fines, pleaded guilty to fraud, and rebranded as Point72 Asset Management.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Firm-level penalties for insider trading can be large but survivable; the franchise persisted under a new name.
insights.quote: SAC Capital paid $1.8 billion in fines and pleaded guilty to fraud charges, and rebranded as Point72 Asset Management.

insights.claim: FINRA's electronic surveillance of NYSE, Nasdaq and OTC trading flagged the archetypal pattern of liquidating a massive long and reversing to short within days before catastrophic news, leading to an SEC referral, FBI involvement, and Gilman's cooperation in exchange for no jail time.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Abrupt long-to-short reversals ahead of binary biotech events are exactly what market surveillance detects; such footprints are both regulatory red flags and potential informed-flow signals.
insights.quote: someone held a massive long position, liquidated the entire thing, and then reversed to a short position all in the span of a few days, right before catastrophic news hit
insights.locator: How did they catch this guy

insights.claim: Accurate pricing of biotech companies is a net social good because capital should flow to good drug developers and away from bad ones, even if some top funds benefit from information nobody else could reasonably have.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Specialist funds serve a capital-allocation role in biotech; their presence improves price discovery but embeds an information asymmetry against other investors.
insights.quote: Good drug developers should get money, bad ones should not get money.
insights.locator: This all said: it would be unfair
